\chapter{Show It To Me: The First Transaction}
\label{ch:mw-show-request}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can point at one thing and ask a shopkeeper, a food seller, or a driver to show it to me, after learning only \mw{ख}.}

A pointing word and an asking word join one already-taught noun, and the resulting request is then run unchanged over a shopping word, a food word, and a transport word in four separately scored skills.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ye]{Hear \emph{ye} — this one}

\label{lesson:MW-C21-hear-ye}



\begin{quote}
Recall the seven-word food payoff, write \textbf{\mw{य}}, then say tea and clothes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ye} — \textbf{this}
\end{quote}

One beat. It points at the single thing in front of you and at nothing else. The source prints it in front of an ordinary noun, exactly the way the next chapters will use it: \emph{ye vastu}, this item.

Every word this book has taught so far names a thing. \emph{ye} does not name anything. It is the first Marwadi word here whose whole job is to pick one out.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye]{\mw{ये} — this, on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C21-ye}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this}, then write tea.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{य}} + \textbf{\mw{े}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{ये}} — \emph{ye} — this
\end{quote}

In \textbf{\mw{चाय}} the glide \textbf{\mw{य}} closed a word and carried no vowel mark. Here the same sign opens a word and carries \textbf{\mw{े}} above the headstroke. One sign, two jobs, and nothing new to learn.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Look at \textbf{\mw{ये}}, cover it, wait five seconds, and write it. Check that \textbf{\mw{े}} sits on top of the headstroke and not beside the stem.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dikhāvo]{Hear \emph{dikhāvo} — show it}

\label{lesson:MW-C21-hear-dikhavo}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\mw{ये}}, then say shop and item and write shop.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{dikhāvo} — \textbf{show it}
\end{quote}

Three beats: \emph{di-khā-vo}, the middle one long. The middle beat carries a breath after the \emph{k} that the \emph{k} of \emph{kapṛā} does not have. Hear both, then say both: \emph{ka} — \emph{khā}.

The source prints this form twice, once for a menu and once for another colour. It is the asking form used to one person across a counter, not a command shouted at anyone, and this lesson teaches the printed form rather than the whole system of asking forms behind it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-6-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 6}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kha]{\mw{ख} — the breathed partner of \mw{क}}

\label{lesson:MW-W21-kha}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{show it}, then write \textbf{\mw{कपड़ा}} and point to its dotted \textbf{\mw{ड़}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — one sign}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ख}} — \emph{kha}
\end{quote}

The sound first, because it is the part a reader can check without a model. Say \textbf{\mw{क}} of \textbf{\mw{कपड़ा}}, then say it again with a puff of breath released on the release: that puff is the whole difference, and it is the difference \textbf{\mw{ख}} records.

The sign is built under the headstroke like every sign so far, with two parts side by side and the vertical stem closing it on the right.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Trace \textbf{\mw{ख}} once and copy it once. Write \textbf{\mw{क}} beside it. Say the pair aloud with a hand in front of your mouth: the breath moves your hand on \textbf{\mw{ख}} and not on \textbf{\mw{क}}. Cover both, wait five seconds, and write \textbf{\mw{ख}} from that breath cue.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dikhāvo]{\mw{दिखावो} — the asking word on the page}

\label{lesson:MW-C21-dikhavo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{show it}, write \textbf{\mw{ख}}, then write wind.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{दि}} + \textbf{\mw{खा}} + \textbf{\mw{वो}} $\to$ \textbf{\mw{दिखावो}} — \emph{dikhāvo} — show it
\end{quote}

Three groups, one for each beat you already hear. \textbf{\mw{ि}} is written before \textbf{\mw{द}} and read after it, the order you first met in \textbf{\mw{मंदिर}}. \textbf{\mw{वो}} is the \textbf{\mw{व}} of \textbf{\mw{हवा}} with the \textbf{\mw{ो}} of \textbf{\mw{घोड़ो}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read the three groups once. Cover the word, wait five seconds, and write it. Check the \textbf{\mw{ि}} stands to the left of \textbf{\mw{द}} and that \textbf{\mw{ख}} carries \textbf{\mw{ा}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Retrieve \emph{this} and \emph{show it}}

\label{lesson:MW-R21-show-two}



\begin{quote}
Recall the seven-word food payoff, then write tea and \textbf{\mw{य}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Hear both words in both orders and give each meaning. Read two cards. Write both from sound, then circle the one sign in them that is new this chapter.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye kapṛā dikhāvo]{Hear \emph{ye kapṛā dikhāvo} — show me this cloth}

\label{lesson:MW-C21-hear-show-request}



\begin{quote}
Say clothes and goods, then write both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\emph{ye kapṛā dikhāvo} — \textbf{show me this cloth}
\end{quote}

Three words, and you already own all three. Point first, name the thing second, ask last: that order does not change when the noun changes.

Hear the line twice. Say it once with your hand out, as if the cloth were on the counter in front of you.

The source prints \emph{dikhāvo} with its own objects. Here it takes a noun this book has already taught, so nothing in the line is unfamiliar except the joining.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ye kapṛā dikhāvo.]{\mw{ये} \mw{कपड़ा} \mw{दिखावो।} — a whole line, no new sign}

\label{lesson:MW-C21-show-request}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{show me this cloth}, then write expensive.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{ये} | \mw{कपड़ा} | \mw{दिखावो।}}
\end{quote}

Three written words, each one already written on its own in an earlier lesson. The full stop is the \textbf{\mw{।}} you first met in \textbf{\mw{पाछे} \mw{मिलसू}}. Nothing here is new but the joining, which is the point of the chapter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read the line once. Cover it for ten seconds and write all three words. Open the model and repair only the word that changed, then rewrite that word alone.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Source: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Payoff — one request, three counters}

\label{lesson:MW-C21-show-three}



\begin{quote}
Recall the seven-word shopping payoff, the five-word transport payoff, and the seven-word food payoff.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
The middle word is the only one that changes.

1. Identify which of the three lines you heard. 2. Produce all three from meaning cues alone. 3. Read three printed lines and say which counter each belongs at. 4. Write all three from dictation, without a model.

Pass each skill separately. Asking to see something is one move; asking what it costs, saying it is too dear, and settling on a price are still untaught.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-6-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 6}; \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-10-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 10}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Close the writing loop for \mw{ख}}

\label{lesson:MW-R21-script-close}



\begin{quote}
Recall the three-counter request payoff, then say rickshaw and flatbread.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Without a model, write four single signs from sound cues: \textbf{\mw{ख}}, \textbf{\mw{य}}, \textbf{\mw{श}}, \textbf{\mw{ट}}. Three of those four have been on the page for chapters without being asked for on their own, which is why they are here.

Then write \textbf{\mw{दिखावो}}, \textbf{\mw{ये}}, \textbf{\mw{रिक्शा}}, \textbf{\mw{रोटी}}, and \textbf{\mw{चाय}} from dictation. Repair only the missed unit and rewrite its word once.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Sources: \href{https://www.marwaripathshala.com/marwari-lesson-9-english}{Marwari Pathshala, Lesson 9}; \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0900.pdf}{Unicode Devanagari chart}.
